title: Ovarian Cancer
subject: Pathology
summary: Ovarian cancer is a malignant epithelial tumour, most often serous cystadenocarcinoma. Diagnosis relies on imaging, tumour markers and histology, and staging follows FIGO. Management combines surgery and platinum‑taxane chemotherapy, adapted to low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A malignant tumour arising from ovarian surface epithelium, most commonly high‑grade serous carcinoma. Diagnosis requires tissue confirmation, usually after imaging identifies a complex adnexal mass.
b: Complex cystic or solid‑cystic ovarian mass on ultrasound or CT
Elevated CA‑125 (supports but not diagnostic)
Histology showing papillary structures with atypia and stromal invasion

sections.p: Staging uses the FIGO system (I‑IV) based on surgical findings of tumour spread.
b: Stage I: confined to ovaries
Stage II: pelvic extension
Stage III: peritoneal implants or lymph nodes
Stage IV: distant metastases (e.g., liver, lung)

sections.p: Most cases are sporadic; hereditary factors dominate the remainder.
b: BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants – highest risk
Family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause
Endometriosis (clear‑cell subtype)
Tobacco, obesity – modest risk

sections.p: Symptoms are vague and often late, leading to delayed presentation in low‑resource settings.
b: Abdominal distension or bloating
Early satiety, weight loss
Pelvic or back pain
Ascites (fluid accumulation)
Irregular vaginal bleeding if tumour invades uterus

t.b: Is the mass cystic, solid, or complex? → Complex solid‑cystic lesions raise suspicion for malignancy.
Is the tumour marker elevated? → High CA‑125 supports ovarian cancer but can be raised in benign conditions; a normal result does not exclude disease.
Is there evidence of spread (peritoneal implants, lymph nodes)? → Guides surgical planning and staging.
Are malignant cells present? → Positive cytology upstages to FIGO III/IV.
What is the histologic subtype? → Determines prognosis and chemotherapy choice.
Is a pathogenic variant present? → Influences counselling, surveillance and eligibility for PARP inhibitors.

sections.p: Complications arise from tumour burden and treatment.
b: Rapidly enlarging abdomen → bowel obstruction
Severe ascites → respiratory compromise
Venous thromboembolism – hypercoagulable state
Chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia → infection risk

sections.p: Goal is maximal cytoreduction followed by systemic therapy; adapt to resource limits.
b: Primary debulking surgery (total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo‑oophorectomy, omentectomy) when operable
Neoadjuvant platinum‑taxane chemotherapy if tumour unresectable
Adjuvant carboplatin + paclitaxel for 6 cycles (standard; avoid if severe neuropathy)
Consider intraperitoneal chemotherapy where expertise exists
Supportive care: manage ascites (paracentesis), pain, nutrition

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence; primary prevention focuses on risk reduction.
b: CA‑125 and clinical exam every 3‑4 months for 2 years, then 6‑monthly
Ultrasound if CA‑125 rises or symptoms recur
Risk‑reducing salpingo‑oophorectomy for BRCA carriers after childbearing
Oral contraceptives reduce risk; counsel on benefits vs. thrombotic risk

sections.p: Other pelvic masses can mimic ovarian cancer.
b: Benign ovarian cysts – usually unilocular, thin‑walled, no solid nodules
Uterine fibroids – arise from uterus, not ovary, and have characteristic shadowing
Tuberculosis pelvic involvement – may cause adnexal mass with caseating necrosis
CA‑125 can be raised in endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, pregnancy
Normal CA‑125 early in disease – do not rule out cancer

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in abdominal girth with pain
New onset shortness of breath from massive ascites
Signs of bowel obstruction (vomiting, no stool passage)

faq.q: Why is CA‑125 not a definitive screening test?
faq.a: It lacks specificity; many benign conditions raise it, and early cancers may have normal levels.
Cure is possible when disease is confined to the ovary (stage I) and complete cytoreduction is achieved.

faq.q: What is the role of BRCA testing in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: It guides counselling and eligibility for targeted therapy, but if unavailable, management follows standard protocols.

exam: What is the next step after finding a complex ovarian mass on ultrasound in a 55‑year‑old woman? — Obtain serum CA‑125 and arrange referral for surgical assessment.
How does FIGO stage III differ from stage II, and why does it change management? — Stage III indicates peritoneal spread or lymph node involvement, prompting neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery.
A patient with known ovarian cancer presents with new ascites; what does a positive cytology mean? — Upstages disease to FIGO III/IV and confirms need for systemic therapy.
Why is platinum‑taxane chemotherapy preferred over single‑agent therapy? — Synergistic DNA damage and microtubule inhibition improve response rates and survival.
In a setting without CT, how would you assess operability? — Use detailed ultrasound, clinical exam for ascites and performance status; consider diagnostic laparoscopy if feasible.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for possible bowel obstruction? — Persistent vomiting with abdominal distension and inability to pass flatus or stool.

How would you counsel a BRCA‑positive woman about risk‑reducing surgery? — Explain that bilateral salpingo‑oophorectomy after childbearing reduces ovarian cancer risk by >80 % and also lowers breast cancer risk.
Why might CA‑125 be normal in early-stage disease, and how does that affect follow‑up? — Small tumour burden may not secrete enough antigen; rely on imaging and clinical exam for surveillance.
